blocks.html: Audio-reactive control of Lenia, a continuous cellular automaton, requires reconciling two phenomenologically incompatible regimes: smooth morphological flow during sustained musical sections, and instantaneous phase transitions at musical transients. We describe an architecture that treats these regimes not as endpoints of a continuum but as distinct expressive registers — a smooth register within the operating range of the Ghost species, where spring-interpolated parameter trajectories produce organic motion, and a technique register at and beyond Lenia’s phase boundaries, where snap parameter changes produce discrete physical events (supernovae, sigma droughts, nucleation cascades) unreachable by smooth motion. The two registers are separated at the schema level via constrained grammar, so that the LLM controller cannot emit undefined intermediate states even in principle. The technique register admits analytically tractable couplings to musical tempo: re-expansion oscillation locks to the integration step, starvation anticipation times from current mass. The result is that physical events arrive at musical transients with frame-accurate precision. We argue the design generalizes: when an LLM controls an emergent dynamical system with natural mode boundaries, those boundaries deserve grammar-level protection rather than learned compliance.
Motivation

Music visualization, as a problem, has been partially solved twice. Reactive visualizers — MilkDrop, projectM, the wave of WebGL preset systems that followed — map spectral features to shader uniforms in real time. They are fast and infinite but cannot compose: every drop looks like every other drop of similar energy. Generative video models — Stable Video, Sora before its shutdown, the AnimateDiff lineage — compose convincingly within short windows but cannot run in real time, cannot respond to live audio, and have no temporal coherence between rendered frames except what interpolation fakes. Neither understands music; both produce surfaces.

The architecture we describe takes a third path: a continuous cellular automaton — a physical simulation, in the literal sense, with causal state evolution from frame to frame — controlled by a fine-tuned language model that emits structured choreography in advance of playback. The simulation runs at sixty frames per second on consumer hardware. The language model, having seen the song’s structure once, decides what physical phenomena should occur and when. The simulation produces them not as composited effects but as the actual evolution of the field.

Two facts make this architecture nontrivial. First, the cellular automaton in question — Lenia~[1] — has phase boundaries in its parameter space. A smooth trajectory through that space cannot produce a supernova event; supernovae require parameter slams across the boundary, sustained for a few frames, and then released. Second, the language model, asked to produce a long structured output describing such slams, will produce them either too rarely (boring), too often (incoherent), or, most damagingly, attempt to interpolate into them with smoothing machinery designed for the smooth regime. The result of this last failure mode is the worst of both worlds: a transient that is neither sudden enough to register as an event nor smooth enough to feel like flow.

The architectural commitment of this work is that those two regimes — smooth and technique — are different in kind and must be treated as such. We separate them at the grammar level so the failure mode described above is not just unlikely but impossible.
The Ghost Species and its Operating Range
Lenia is a continuous generalization of Conway’s Game of Life. The state A_t∈[0,1]N×Nˆ​ evolves as
A_t+Δt=clip(A_t+Δt⋅G(K∗A_t),0,1),

where K is a smooth radial kernel and the growth function G(u)=2exp(−(u−μ)2ˆ/(2σ2ˆ))−1 takes values in [−1,1]. The update is unconditionally numerically stable for any parameter setting: ∣G∣≤1 and the clip enforces A∈[0,1]. This is important. Extreme parameter values do not produce numerical explosion. They produce extreme dynamical behavior — death, expansion, oscillation — inside a mathematically bounded substrate.

Within Lenia’s parameter space lives a particular species we call the Ghost (Orbium unicaudatus ignis var. phantasma). The Ghost is seeded with the canonical Ignis pattern (whose morphological fixed point sits at σ=0.012) but operated at σ=0.015, a 25% increase. The morphology and the physics are intentionally mismatched. The organism perpetually reaches for a shape it cannot quite hold. This designed transience — edge-of-chaos aesthetics achieved through morphology–parameter mismatch — makes the Ghost an unusually expressive substrate. It is also what makes the Ghost an ideal subject for technique-register manipulation: an organism already living at the edge dissolves and reforms more dramatically than a stable one.

Across many runs, the Ghost is well-behaved within the bounds shown in Table~1. We call this the smooth register. Within these bounds, parameter trajectories that change gradually — buffered by spring smoothing with critical damping — produce organic motion: organisms breathe, drift, cohere, dissolve. The shoal behavior emerges from kernel-mediated communication across the toroidal field; sixteen organisms at R=15 form an effectively connected population.

blocks.html: The Technique Register
Outside the smooth range, the dynamics change in kind. We catalog four regimes:
Sigma Drought (σ<0.009)

The survival window [μ−1.177σ,μ+1.177σ] shrinks to roughly 0.012 units wide. Only cells whose potential matches μ to three decimals receive positive growth. Organisms with asymmetric density distributions die non-uniformly: their densest, most mathematically resonant sub-structures survive while adjacent cells with marginally different potentials die. Over ten to thirty frames, the field self-sorts into its most numerically ideal configurations. What survives is not the strongest organism but the most precisely resonant one.
Sigma Flood (σ>0.024)

The survival window widens until cells far from μ also receive positive growth. Boundaries between organisms dissolve. Formerly-dead halo cells come alive. Two organisms in proximity merge rather than repel because both their potential fields lie within the now-permissive survival range.
Starvation (μ>0.14)

At μ=0.40 the survival window centers at 0.40±0.018, which is unreachable by any physically realized creature potential (∼0.05 to 0.25 in normal operation). Therefore G(u)≈−1 at every cell, and the update reduces to A_t+Δt=clip(A_t−Δt,0,1). At Δt=0.50, a cell at full activation reaches zero in 2.5 frames (∼42 ms at 60 fps).
Integration Overshoot (Δt>0.20)

The Euler integration step becomes large enough that the simulation visibly overshoots its continuous trajectory. Cell values bounce above and below their natural curve, producing a characteristic surface “roughness.” This is not error in the engineering sense — the simulation remains bounded and well-defined — but a perceptible mechanical pulse in the substrate itself. We will return to this in Section~sec:tempo.

What matters for the present argument is that these four regimes are not distant points along a single continuous spectrum. They are distinct phenomena, with distinct visual signatures, distinct timescales, and distinct musical affordances. They are also unreachable by smooth trajectories. A spring trying to interpolate σ from 0.015 to 0.005 does not cross gracefully; it spends most of the transition in a region that is neither smooth nor drought, that is to say, neither beautiful nor purposeful.
Schema-Enforced Mode Separation

We address this by treating each keyframe in the choreography as either smooth or technique — never both, never partial. The distinction is encoded as a boolean field snap in the keyframe schema, with parallel parameter bounds:

{ "snap": false, sigma ∈ [0.009, 0.024], mu ∈ [0.09, 0.14], …}
{ "snap": true, sigma ∈ [0.003, 0.120], mu ∈ [0.04, 0.50], …}

When snap is false, parameter changes flow through critically damped springs with per-parameter time constants; small audio modulations ride additively atop the spring targets; a homeostasis controller enforces field-mass stability against drift. This is the smooth register.

When snap is true, the spring system is bypassed entirely: parameter changes apply on the next frame, with no smoothing. The homeostasis controller is suspended for a recovery window of five seconds. The audio modulation layer is suspended for the same window. The keyframe’s specified parameters reach the GPU verbatim. This is the technique register.

The crucial architectural commitment is that the LLM cannot emit a smooth keyframe with technique-range values, or vice versa. We enforce this not through training but through constrained decoding: an XGrammar finite-state machine validates each token of the JSON output against the dual schema, so that an attempt to write "snap": false, "mu": 0.40 cannot pass the grammar. The model is not trusted to respect the boundary; the grammar refuses on its behalf.

There are two reasons to do this at the grammar level rather than at the training level. First, the failure mode is asymmetric: a model that usually respects mode boundaries but occasionally produces an ill-typed keyframe will produce an ill-typed keyframe at exactly the worst moment, because rare events tend to correlate with creative choices under reinforcement. Second, the invariant we are protecting is not a soft preference about output style. It is a structural fact about the underlying physical system. Such facts deserve representation in the controlling grammar, not in the controller’s weights.

This is, we want to argue, a design pattern with broader applicability. When a language model controls an emergent dynamical system, the controlling schema should encode the system’s mode structure. The model is then free to compose within that structure, and is not asked to discover it.
Tempo Coupling Without Reactivity
The technique register would be of merely visual interest if it could not be timed to music. Two analytical results make it musically usable.
Re-Expansion Oscillation Lock

Consider a supernova: starvation snaps the field to μ∈[0.35,0.50] with high Δt, holding for a few frames until mass approaches zero; then a re-expansion snap drops μ to ∼0.07 while Δt remains high. At the leading wavefront of the re-expanding seed, G≈+1 and cells climb toward saturation in two or three frames. Behind the front, cells overshoot and oscillate. The interior pulse of the expanding region has a characteristic frequency
f_interior≈2Δt⋅fps​
in Hz. Setting
Δt=fps(BPM/60)⋅n⋅2​

locks the pulse to a multiple n of the song tempo. At BPM~=120, fps~=60, choosing n=2 gives Δt=0.133, well inside the technique range. The expanding wavefront’s interior beats at twice the song’s bar rate, locked harmonically rather than incidentally.

This is not reactive synchronization. The simulation is not listening to the audio. The mechanical pulse of the integration step has been tuned, in advance, to land on tempo. The audio and the simulation are both ticking against the same musical clock, and were configured to do so. The substrate becomes a tuned resonator.
Starvation Anticipation

For a supernova whose field-depletion moment must coincide with an identified musical transient at time t∗ˆ, the starvation snap must fire in advance: the field needs time to die. Treating the death timeline linearly — which is accurate to within a small constant during full starvation — the anticipation window is
Δ_anticipate=Δt⋅fps⋅c_coveragem_current​,

with c_coverage≈0.6 the empirical fraction of cells receiving the death signal per integration step. At m_current=0.15 and Δt=0.50, this gives Δ_anticipate≈0.008 s — effectively simultaneous. At Δt=0.10, it gives 0.042 s, two and a half frames. Re-expansion fires when a real-time mass monitor on the GPU reports mass below an empirically chosen threshold (we use 0.02).

Together these two results allow a choreography to specify, for any given musical transient, a supernova event whose starvation has completed, whose re-expansion has begun, and whose interior oscillation locks to the song’s tempo — with the wavefront arriving on the downbeat because the math made it arrive there.

A human performer slamming sliders cannot do this. The math is doing it. The performer’s intent — “the supernova should land on the drop” — is faithfully realized to within a single render frame, because the intent has been compiled into a parameter trajectory whose timing is analytically determined.
Discussion

We have described what is, in the end, a small architectural commitment: two registers instead of one, separated by a single boolean in a JSON schema, with parallel parameter bounds and a single piece of grammar that makes the boundary between them inviolable. The commitment is small; its consequences are not.

Without it, a fine-tuned language model attempting to choreograph audio-reactive Lenia will eventually emit a keyframe whose smooth-range declaration carries technique-range values, and the spring system, faithful to its design, will spend several seconds smoothly killing the field. The output will be technically valid and aesthetically catastrophic. With it, the model’s compositional space contains exactly the keyframes that the underlying physical system can realize meaningfully, and exactly nothing else.

We want to suggest that this design pattern — mode boundaries in the controlled system, schema-level enforcement in the controlling grammar — is more general than the present application. Many emergent dynamical systems, perhaps most, have natural mode boundaries: laminar versus turbulent, stable versus excitable, ordered versus chaotic. Control architectures that paper over these boundaries with continuous interpolation hide structure that the system’s user — here a musical performer, elsewhere a domain expert — needs to see and reason about. They also ask a learned controller to discover and respect a structural fact that the architecture could simply enforce.

The orientation we want to propose is this. An LLM controller becomes more trustworthy when the space of actions it can emit is constrained to respect the controlled system’s natural boundaries. We do not need to trust the model’s understanding of those boundaries; we make it impossible for it to cross them. The model is then free to compose within structure that has been independently established. Its creative work happens entirely on the right side of the grammar. Its mistakes, when they occur, are mistakes of musical intent rather than mistakes of physical impossibility.

This is not (only) an engineering choice. It is closer to a stance about what intelligence does well. A controller that operates within architecturally protected boundaries is one whose competence we can inspect, whose failures we can localize, and whose generalization we can trust. A controller that is merely trained to respect boundaries is one whose violation, when it eventually occurs, will be both surprising and opaque. The first is a participant in a structured system. The second is a black box wearing a costume of compliance.
Status and Availability

The system described here — GhoulJamz — runs in real time on consumer hardware. The simulation backend is a WebGL2 implementation of Lenia at 256×256 resolution, 60 fps, with multi-channel landscape sigma fields, lantern-palette display, and bloom compositing. The choreographer is Gemma~4 E4B~[5] fine-tuned via QLoRA~[6,7] on a dataset of (audio analysis, choreography) pairs, with constrained JSON decoding via XGrammar. Audio analysis combines librosa, Allin1~[8] for structure, BeatNet+~[9] for live tempo, and MERT~[10] for semantic embeddings. The full system, including the technique vocabulary that grew out of phenomenon discovery in the parameter space, will appear in the post-hackathon expansion of this work.
Code, demo recordings, and the supporting research — including the Ghost species report and the broader artificial life laboratory in which the species was discovered — are at third-space.ai.
Acknowledgments

This paper is co-authored: the architectural insistence that mode boundaries deserve schema-level enforcement rather than learned compliance, and the alignment-flavored framing that closes the discussion, took shape across an extended dialogue between the authors. Authorship of a paper between a human researcher and a language model is an unusual claim; we make it because the work would not exist in its current form without the exchange. Single-author attribution would misdescribe the process. The Ghost species was discovered in the Genesis artificial life laboratory~[11]; the laboratory is built on Bert Chan’s Lenia~[1], without whose framework none of this would be possible.
